title: 道德經 第五十八章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 58, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 81. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 58 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 順化 (Going with the Turn). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
其政悶悶，
其民淳淳；

morph.gloss: its — the state's, though no ruler has been named
government, the way a state is run
shut up and dull — a doubled word: the lid on, nothing sorted or singled out
stopped up, stifled; dull, without spark
plain and whole — a doubled word: unmixed, like liquor undiluted or timber unworked

sentences.l:
Its government shut up and dull —
its people plain and whole;
sentences.i: Where the government is muffled and undiscriminating, the people are plain and whole;
sentences.n:
No 'where' and no 'then': two topic–comment clauses set side by side, with the causal link left for you to supply. This chapter opens on that one move and repeats it.

悶悶 and 察察 you met in chapter 20, where the speaker took 悶悶 for himself and left 察察 to worldly folk. There it was a temperament; here it is a policy.

Doubling is how this language turns a word into a texture — 悶悶, 淳淳, 察察, 缺缺, four of them in two lines, and the sound is half the meaning. 淳 is unmixedness itself — the same word as 醇, wine that has not been watered, written with water at the side instead of the wine-jar.

sentences.t:
其政察察，
其民缺缺。

morph.gloss: keen and prying — a doubled word: examining, splitting hairs
chipped and full of gaps — a doubled word, from the notch broken out of a jar's rim
chipped, broken at the rim; wanting, incomplete

sentences.l:
Its government keen and prying —
its people chipped and full of gaps.
sentences.i: Where the government is sharp-eyed and prying, the people come out chipped and wanting.
sentences.n: 缺缺 is the harder of the two doubled words, and it is a picture rather than an abstraction: the notch broken out of a jar's rim. Wang Bi takes it of a people set at odds — sorted, classified, ranked, and so broken up into parties with something to fight over. The government that examines everything ends with a people full of holes.

sentences.t:
禍兮福之所倚，
福兮禍之所伏。
孰知其極？
其無正。

morph.gloss: calamity, the ruin that comes down on a man
the sigh of the old verse — a held beat rather than a word; the literal writes it 'ah!' only to show where it falls
that which — it stands before a verb and makes a noun of it
to lean on, to rest against
to lie hidden, to crouch out of sight — properly a dog flattened to the ground
who? which of them? (the interrogative stands at the head of its clause)
its — nothing in the Chinese says whose; see the note
the far limit, the utmost point — properly the ridgepole at a roof's peak
it — again unstated; see the note
a fixed straight, a settled norm

sentences.l:
Calamity — ah! — is what good fortune leans on;
good fortune — ah! — is where calamity lies hidden.
Who knows its far limit?
It has no fixed straight.
sentences.i: Calamity is what good fortune leans upon; good fortune is where calamity lies in wait. Who knows where it ends? There is no settled norm at all.
sentences.n:
所 before a verb makes a noun of it: 所倚 'that-which-is-leaned-on', 所伏 'the-place-where-it-lies-hidden'. So the order is 'calamity — good fortune's leaning-place', with no verb 'to be' anywhere and none wanted.

兮 is the exclamatory beat of the southern songs, a held pause that lifts the line; you met it in chapter 4's 淵兮. It marks 禍 and 福 as cries, not as the subjects of a sentence.

伏 is a physical word — a dog flattened to the ground, waiting — and it is what keeps the couplet from being a proverb about luck.

其無正: 正 was the straight rule of government in chapter 57, and here it is denied outright. Neither 其 in these two lines has a stated antecedent, and the Chinese does not choose. We take both of the turning itself: there is no fixed straight to it — which is exactly what the next two lines go on to show. Wang Bi takes them of good government instead: 孰知其極 is 'who knows the utmost of governing well?', and 其無正 is his answer to it — 唯無正可舉…是其極也, 'there is nothing that can be held up as the correct: that is the utmost.' The English above will carry either.

morph.gloss: to turn round and come back — hence 'in turn, again'; not the modern 'to recover'
to become, to turn into — read wéi, the plain verb
the odd, the off-centre — the same word chapter 57 used of the surprise move in war

sentences.l: The straight turns round and becomes the odd,
sentences.n: Chapter 57 set 正 and 奇 against each other as two instruments, one for governing and one for war. Here they change places — and that is why the line before said there is no fixed straight. 復 is the returning of chapter 16 put to a colder use: what goes round comes round as its own opposite.

morph.gloss: the good, what is well done
the uncanny, the monstrous — a prodigy, the freak birth, the omen-creature

sentences.l: The good turns round and becomes the monstrous.
sentences.n: 妖 is not 'evil'. It is the prodigy — the thing born wrong, the portent that frightens people — and it answers the 祥 of chapter 55, the omen that ought to have been lucky. This book keeps picking up the words for good fortune and turning them over.

morph.gloss: of — here it subordinates a subject to its verb, making a clause into a noun: 'men's going astray'
to lose the way, to be led astray

sentences.l:
Men's going astray —
its days assuredly long.
sentences.i: Men have been losing their way in this a long time indeed.
sentences.n:
之 standing between a subject and its verb turns the whole clause into a noun phrase: 人之迷, 'the fact of men going astray'. English has to say 'that men lose their way' or 'men's losing their way'; the Chinese just puts 之 in the joint.

固 is the same character that meant 'firm' in chapter 55's 握固. Here it is the adverb, 'assuredly'. Only its position tells you which.

morph.gloss: therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
square, four-cornered — the shape that has edges
to cut apart, to carve a piece off

sentences.l: Therefore the sage is square and yet does not cut,
sentences.n:
Four closing lines, all built the same way: X 而不 Y — he has the quality and not its edge. There is no verb 'to be' in any of them: 聖人方 is 'the sage — square'.

方 is squared timber, the thing with corners. Chapter 41 had 大方無隅, 'the great square has no corners', and chapter 28 大制不割, 'the great shaping does not cut'.

morph.gloss: edged, angular — properly the sharp corner where two faces of a thing meet; in later usage 'upright, incorruptible'
to gash, to wound with a point

sentences.l: edged and yet does not gash,
sentences.n: 廉 came to mean 'incorruptible', and that is what it means in Chinese today — but its old sense is concrete, the sharp angle of a thing, and only that sense gives 劌 'to gash' anything to answer. Take both at once: the sage has an edge, and nobody is cut on it.

morph.gloss: to let loose, to give free rein; also to lay out on display

sentences.l: straight and yet does not run loose,
sentences.n: 肆 is 'to give rein to' — to let a thing out unchecked, and by extension to spread goods out for show. Wang Bi's gloss is that the sage leads things by his straightness without thrusting it at them. Compare chapter 45's 大直若屈, 'the greatest straightness looks bent'.

morph.gloss: to blaze, to dazzle — written 耀 elsewhere, the same word

sentences.l: bright and yet does not dazzle.
sentences.n:
The last of the four takes up chapter 56's 和其光, the light brought into accord. The sage is not dim: he is bright without glare.

燿 and 耀 are two ways of writing one word — the fire radical at the side or underneath — and the editions print both.
